rv.q: This magnificent piece of theatre, first staged here in 2019, now returns even better than before: a story about who we are and how we got here, told on the biggest stage of the National Theatre.
Norris’s whirligig, beautifully acted production makes extravagant use of the Olivier’s theatrical toy box while remaining clean and uncluttered.
Edmundson captures the broad sweep of the novel's themes as well as its comedy.
If Small Island appears to have taken a place in the National Theatre’s pantheon already, it is with good reason.
Having flattened out the complexities of the book, Edmundson leaves us with a plodding narrative: you could call it the Ladybird Guide to Racial Prejudice.
This revival with a new cast is utterly sensational – an engrossing, all-embracing piece of theatre.
The visual ingenuity is underpinned by storytelling as deft as it is emotionally powerful, scored through with wit and poignancy.
A powerful, important and relevant production.
Levy’s tale, and Edmundson’s well-crafted retelling, leaves its protagonists with decades of our history still in their future.
This welcome revival of a much-praised show first seen at the National in 2019 is an entertaining, gentle, believable slice of English and Jamaican history that should be told.
Overall, Small Island is theatre at its best.
This brilliant play explores the injustices faced by the people who arrived on our shores in the 1940s in search of a better life, only to be met with violence and hostility.

cn.t: Critics widely praise this Windrush-era epic as magnificent, sweeping theatre, with standout performances and Edmundson's adaptation lauded for balancing intimacy with scale. A lone dissenter finds it overly simplistic.
